stem: The five-kingdom system of classification was proposed in 1969 by
explanation: Whittaker placed organisms in Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, using cell type, level of organisation and mode of nutrition. Linnaeus used two kingdoms, Haeckel added a third (Protista) and Chatton introduced the prokaryote-eukaryote division.

stem: In the scientific name Mangifera indica (mango), written by binomial nomenclature, the word Mangifera is the name of the
explanation: In the binomial system of Linnaeus the first word, written with a capital letter, is the genus and the second word, in small letters, is the species epithet. Family and order are higher ranks that do not appear in the two-word name.

stem: The protein coat that surrounds the nucleic acid of a virus is called the
explanation: The capsid is made of protein subunits called capsomeres and encloses the viral DNA or RNA. Some viruses also have an outer lipid envelope taken from the host membrane, while a capsule and a cell wall are bacterial structures.

stem: In the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage, the final stage is
options: joining of the phage DNA into the host chromosome
division of the host cell carrying a prophage
lysis of the host cell, releasing many new phages
attachment of the phage tail to the host wall
explanation: After the phage DNA takes over the cell and new phages are assembled, the host cell bursts (lyses) and releases them. Integration of phage DNA as a prophage and its copying during host division belong to the lysogenic cycle, and attachment is the first step.

stem: HIV weakens the immune system mainly by destroying
options: plasma B cells of the spleen
explanation: HIV binds to the CD4 receptor found on helper T cells, multiplies inside them and kills them, so both cell-mediated and antibody responses fail. Red cells and platelets have no CD4 receptor and are not its target.

stem: A retrovirus such as HIV can insert its genes into host DNA because it carries the enzyme
explanation: Reverse transcriptase uses the viral RNA as a template to make a DNA copy, which then becomes integrated into the host chromosome. Restriction enzymes cut DNA and come from bacteria, not retroviruses.

stem: Which type of viral hepatitis is spread mainly through contaminated food and water?
explanation: Hepatitis A virus is shed in faeces and spreads by the faecal-oral route where sanitation is poor. Hepatitis B, C and D spread through blood and body fluids, such as unscreened transfusions and reused syringes.
Bacteria are named by shape: bacilli are rods, cocci are spheres, spirilla are spirals and vibrios are comma-shaped. Cocci is the usual confusion because the words are often learned together.

stem: Gram-positive bacteria appear purple after Gram staining because they have
options: an outer lipid membrane that absorbs the safranin counterstain
a thick peptidoglycan wall that retains crystal violet
explanation: The thick peptidoglycan layer of Gram-positive bacteria holds the crystal violet-iodine complex even after alcohol washing. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer under an outer membrane, lose the violet and take up the pink safranin counterstain.

stem: Endospores are formed by some bacteria mainly to
explanation: One cell forms only one endospore, a tough, dormant structure resistant to heat and drying, which germinates when conditions improve. Because one cell gives one spore, it is a survival method, not reproduction, which is done by binary fission.

stem: In the cyanobacterium Nostoc, nitrogen fixation takes place in special thick-walled cells called
explanation: Heterocysts lack the oxygen-producing photosystem and have thick walls, which protect the oxygen-sensitive enzyme nitrogenase. Akinetes are resting spores and hormogonia are short fragments used in reproduction.

stem: Malaria is caused by the protist Plasmodium, which is transmitted to humans by the bite of
explanation: Only female mosquitoes suck blood, and Plasmodium completes part of its life cycle in the female Anopheles. Aedes mosquitoes spread dengue virus, not malaria.

stem: Which protist is correctly matched with its structure for locomotion?
explanation: Paramecium beats thousands of short cilia, Amoeba moves by pseudopodia and Euglena uses a flagellum. Plasmodium is a non-motile parasite in most stages, so the other pairings swap or invent structures.

stem: The cell wall of most fungi is mainly composed of
explanation: Fungal walls contain chitin, a nitrogen-containing polysaccharide also found in the exoskeleton of insects. Cellulose is the plant wall material and peptidoglycan is found in bacteria.

stem: A bacteriophage injects its DNA into a bacterium, but the cell does not burst; instead, all its descendants for many generations carry the phage DNA. This shows that the phage is in the
options: lytic cycle, at the assembly stage
explanation: In lysogeny the phage DNA joins the host chromosome as a prophage and is copied with it at each division, so daughter cells inherit it without being destroyed. In the lytic cycle new phages are made at once and the host bursts within a short time.

stem: Prions, which cause diseases such as mad cow disease, are infectious particles made of
explanation: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause normal copies of the same protein to misfold, and they contain no nucleic acid. Viroids, by contrast, are short naked RNA molecules, and viruses contain nucleic acid inside a protein coat.

stem: A bacterium with many flagella distributed all over its surface is described as
explanation: Peritrichous means flagella around the whole cell. Monotrichous is a single flagellum, lophotrichous is a tuft at one end and amphitrichous is a flagellum or tuft at each end.

stem: Penicillin kills many bacteria but does not harm human cells because it
options: destroys the 80S ribosomes that are found only in bacterial cells
blocks the synthesis of peptidoglycan, which human cells lack
dissolves the nuclear membrane of bacteria
blocks the cellulose cell wall of bacteria
explanation: Penicillin prevents the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so growing bacteria form weak walls and burst; human cells have no cell wall, so they are unaffected. Bacteria have 70S ribosomes and no nuclear membrane, and their walls are not made of cellulose.
